Happy is the man that feareth alay; But he that hardeneth his heart shall fall into mischief.
\add As\add* a roaring lion, and a ranging bear, \add So is\add* a icked ruler over a poor people.
The prince that lacketh understanding is also a great oppressor; \add But\add* he that hateth covetousness shall prolong his days.
A man that is laden ith the blood of any person Shall flee unto the pit; let no man stay him.
Whoso alketh uprightly shall be delivered; But he that is perverse in \add his\add* ays shall fall at once.
He that tilleth his land shall have plenty of bread; But he that folloeth after vain \add persons\add* shall have poverty enough.
A faithful man shall abound ith blessings; But he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be unpunished.
To have respect of persons is not good; Neither that a man should transgress for a piece of bread.
He that hath an evil eye hasteth after riches, And knoeth not that ant shall come upon him.
He that rebuketh a man shall afterard find more favor Than he that flattereth ith the tongue.
Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith, It is no transgression, The same is the companion of a destroyer.
He that is of a greedy spirit stirreth up strife; But he that putteth his trust in Jehovah shall be made fat.
He that trusteth in his on heart is a fool; But hoso alketh isely, he shall be delivered.
He that giveth unto the poor shall not lack; But he that hideth his eyes shall have many a curse.
When the icked rise, men hide themselves; But hen they perish, the righteous increase.
He that being often reproved hardeneth his neck Shall suddenly be destroyed, and that ithout remedy.
When the righteous are increased, the people rejoice; But hen a icked man beareth rule, the people sigh.
Whoso loveth isdom rejoiceth his father; But he that keepeth company ith harlots asteth \add his\add* substance.
The king by justice establisheth the land; But he that exacteth gifts overthroeth it.
A man that flattereth his neighbor Spreadeth a net for his steps.
In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare; But the righteous doth sing and rejoice.
The righteous taketh knoledge of the cause of the poor; The icked hath not understanding to kno \add it\add*.
Scoffers set a city in a flame; But ise men turn aay rath.
If a ise man hath a controversy ith a foolish man, Whether he be angry or laugh, there ill be no rest.
The bloodthirsty hate him that is perfect; And as for the upright, they seek his life.
A fool uttereth all his anger; But a ise man keepeth it back and stilleth it.
If a ruler hearkeneth to falsehood, All his servants are icked.
The poor man and the oppressor meet together; Jehovah lighteneth the eyes of them both.
The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, His throne shall be established for ever.
The rod and reproof give isdom; But a child left to himself causeth shame to his mother.
When the icked are increased, transgression increaseth; But the righteous shall look upon their fall.
Correct thy son, and he ill give thee rest; Yea, he ill give delight unto thy soul.
Where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint; But he that keepeth the la, happy is he.
A servant ill not be corrected by ords; For though he understand, he ill not give heed.
Seest thou a man that is hasty in his ords? There is more hope of a fool than of him.
He that delicately bringeth up his servant from a child Shall have him become a son at the last.
An angry man stirreth up strife, And a rathful man aboundeth in transgression.
A man’s pride shall bring him lo; But he that is of a loly spirit shall obtain honor.
Whoso is partner ith a thief hateth his on soul; He heareth the adjuration and uttereth nothing.
The fear of man bringeth a snare; But hoso putteth his trust in Jehovah shall be safe.
Many seek the ruler’s favor; But a man’s judgment \add cometh\add* from Jehovah.
An unjust man is an abomination to the righteous; And he that is upright in the ay is an abomination to the icked. \b
The ords of Agur the son of Jakeh; the oracle. \b The man saith unto Ithiel, unto Ithiel and Ucal:
Surely I am more brutish than any man, And have not the understanding of a man;
And I have not learned isdom, Neither have I the knoledge of the Holy One.

Who hath ascended up into heaven, and descended? Who hath gathered the ind in his fists? Who hath bound the aters in his garment? Who hath established all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and hat is his son’s name, if thou knoest? \b
Every ord of God is tried: He is a shield unto them that take refuge in him.
Add thou not unto his ords, Lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar. \b
To things have I asked of thee; Deny me \add them\add* not before I die:
Remove far from me falsehood and lies; Give me neither poverty nor riches; Feed me ith the food that is needful for me:
Lest I be full, and deny \add thee\add*, and say, Who is Jehovah? Or lest I be poor, and steal, And use profanely the name of my God. \b
Slander not a servant unto his master, Lest he curse thee, and thou be held guilty. \b
There is a generation that curse their father, And bless not their mother.
There is a generation that are pure in their on eyes, And \add yet\add* are not ashed from their filthiness.
There is a generation, oh ho lofty are their eyes! And their eyelids are lifted up.
There is a generation hose teeth are \add as\add* sords, and their ja teeth \add as\add* knives, To devour the poor from off the earth, and the needy from among men. \b
The horseleach hath to daughters, \add crying\add*, Give, give. There are three things that are never satisfied, \add Yea\add*, four that say not, Enough:
Sheol; and the barren omb; The earth that is not satisfied ith ater; And the fire that saith not, Enough.
The eye that mocketh at his father, And despiseth to obey his mother, The ravens of the valley shall pick it out, And the young eagles shall eat it. \b
There are three things hich are too onderful for me, Yea, four hich I kno not:
The ay of an eagle in the air; The ay of a serpent upon a rock; The ay of a ship in the midst of the sea; And the ay of a man ith a maiden.
So is the ay of an adulterous oman; She eateth, and ipeth her mouth, And saith, I have done no ickedness. \b
For three things the earth doth tremble, And for four, \add hich\add* it cannot bear:
For a servant hen he is king; And a fool hen he is filled ith food;
For an odious oman hen she is married; And a handmaid that is heir to her mistress. \b
There are four things hich are little upon the earth, But they are exceeding ise:
The ants are a people not strong, Yet they provide their food in the summer;
The conies are but a feeble folk, Yet make they their houses in the rocks;
The locusts have no king, Yet go they forth all of them by bands;
The lizard taketh hold ith her hands, Yet is she in kings’ palaces. \b
There are three things hich are stately in their march, Yea, four hich are stately in going:
The lion, hich is mightiest among beasts, And turneth not aay for any;
The greyhound; the he-goat also; And the king against hom there is no rising up. \b
If thou hast done foolishly in lifting up thyself, Or if thou hast thought evil, \add Lay\add* thy hand upon thy mouth.
For the churning of milk bringeth forth butter, And the ringing of the nose bringeth forth blood; So the forcing of rath bringeth forth strife. \b
The ords of king Lemuel; the oracle hich his mother taught him. \b
What, my son? and hat, O son of my omb? And hat, O son of my vos?
Give not thy strength unto omen, Nor thy ays to that hich destroyeth kings.
It is not for kings, O Lemuel, it is not for kings to drink ine; Nor for princes \add to say\add*, Where is strong drink?
Lest they drink, and forget the la, And pervert the justice \add due\add* to any that is afflicted.
Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, And ine unto the bitter in soul:
Let him drink, and forget his poverty, And remember his misery no more.
Open thy mouth for the dumb, In the cause of all such as are left desolate.
Open thy mouth, judge righteously, And minister justice to the poor and needy. \b
A orthy oman ho can find? For her price is far above rubies.
The heart of her husband trusteth in her, And he shall have no lack of gain.
She doeth him good and not evil All the days of her life.
She seeketh ool and flax, And orketh illingly ith her hands.
She is like the merchant-ships; She bringeth her bread from afar.
She riseth also hile it is yet night, And giveth food to her household, And their task to her maidens.
She considereth a field, and buyeth it; With the fruit of her hands she planteth a vineyard.
She girdeth her loins ith strength, And maketh strong her arms.
She perceiveth that her merchandise is profitable; Her lamp goeth not out by night.
She layeth her hands to the distaff, And her hands hold the spindle.
She stretcheth out her hand to the poor; Yea, she reacheth forth her hands to the needy.
She is not afraid of the sno for her household; For all her household are clothed ith scarlet.
She maketh for herself carpets of tapestry; Her clothing is fine linen and purple.
Her husband is knon in the gates, When he sitteth among the elders of the land.
She maketh linen garments and selleth them, And delivereth girdles unto the merchant.
Strength and dignity are her clothing; And she laugheth at the time to come.
She openeth her mouth ith isdom; And the la of kindness is on her tongue.
She looketh ell to the ays of her household, And eateth not the bread of idleness.
Her children rise up, and call her blessed; Her husband \add also\add*, and he praiseth her, \add saying\add*:
Many daughters have done orthily, But thou excellest them all.
Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain; \add But\add* a oman that feareth Jehovah, she shall be praised.
Give her of the fruit of her hands; And let her orks praise her in the gates.
The ords of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.
Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; vanity of vanities, all is vanity.
What profit hath man of all his labor herein he laboreth under the sun?
One generation goeth, and another generation cometh; but the earth abideth for ever.
The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth don, and hasteth to its place here it ariseth.
The ind goeth toard the south, and turneth about unto the north; it turneth about continually in its course, and the ind returneth again to its circuits.
All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full; unto the place hither the rivers go, thither they go again.
All things are full of eariness; man cannot utter \add it\add*: the eye is not satisfied ith seeing, nor the ear filled ith hearing.
That hich hath been is that hich shall be; and that hich hath been done is that hich shall be done: and there is no ne thing under the sun.
Is there a thing hereof it may be said, See, this is ne? it hath been long ago, in the ages hich ere before us.
There is no remembrance of the former \add generations\add*; neither shall there be any remembrance of the latter \add generations\add* that are to come, among those that shall come after.
I the Preacher as king over Israel in Jerusalem.
And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by isdom concerning all that is done under heaven: it is a sore travail that God hath given to the sons of men to be exercised thereith.
I have seen all the orks that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and a striving after ind.
That hich is crooked cannot be made straight; and that hich is anting cannot be numbered.
I communed ith mine on heart, saying, Lo, I have gotten me great isdom above all that ere before me in Jerusalem; yea, my heart hath had great experience of isdom and knoledge.
And I applied my heart to kno isdom, and to kno madness and folly: I perceived that this also as a striving after ind.
For in much isdom is much grief; and he that increaseth knoledge increaseth sorro.
I said in my heart, Come no, I ill prove thee ith mirth; therefore enjoy pleasure: and, behold, this also as vanity.
I said of laughter, It is mad; and of mirth, What doeth it?

I searched in my heart ho to cheer my flesh ith ine, my heart yet guiding \add me\add* ith isdom, and ho to lay hold on folly, till I might see hat it as good for the sons of men that they should do under heaven all the days of their life.
I made me great orks; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards;
I made me gardens and parks, and I planted trees in them of all kinds of fruit;
I made me pools of ater, to ater therefrom the forest here trees ere reared;
I bought men-servants and maid-servants, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of herds and flocks, above all that ere before me in Jerusalem;

I gathered me also silver and gold, and the treasure of kings and of the provinces; I gat me men-singers and omen-singers, and the delights of the sons of men, musical instruments, and that of all sorts.
So I as great, and increased more than all that ere before me in Jerusalem: also my isdom remained ith me.
And hatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them; I ithheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced because of all my labor; and this as my portion from all my labor.
Then I looked on all the orks that my hands had rought, and on the labor that I had labored to do; and, behold, all as vanity and a striving after ind, and there as no profit under the sun.
And I turned myself to behold isdom, and madness, and folly: for hat \add can\add* the man \add do\add* that cometh after the king? \add even\add* that hich hath been done long ago.
Then I sa that isdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness.
The ise man’s eyes are in his head, and the fool alketh in darkness: and yet I perceived that one event happeneth to them all.
Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so ill it happen even to me; and hy as I then more ise? Then said I in my heart, that this also is vanity.
For of the ise man, even as of the fool, there is no remembrance for ever; seeing that in the days to come all ill have been long forgotten. And ho doth the ise man die even as the fool!
So I hated life, because the ork that is rought under the sun as grievous unto me; for all is vanity and a striving after ind.
And I hated all my labor herein I labored under the sun, seeing that I must leave it unto the man that shall be after me.
And ho knoeth hether he ill be a ise man or a fool? yet ill he have rule over all my labor herein I have labored, and herein I have shoed myself ise under the sun. This also is vanity.
Therefore I turned about to cause my heart to despair concerning all the labor herein I had labored under the sun.
For there is a man hose labor is ith isdom, and ith knoledge, and ith skilfulness; yet to a man that hath not labored therein shall he leave it for his portion. This also is vanity and a great evil.
For hat hath a man of all his labor, and of the striving of his heart, herein he laboreth under the sun?
For all his days are \add but\add* sorros, and his travail is grief; yea, even in the night his heart taketh no rest. This also is vanity.
There is nothing better for a man \add than\add* that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I sa, that it is from the hand of God.
For ho can eat, or ho can have enjoyment, more than I?

For to the man that pleaseth him \add God\add* giveth isdom, and knoledge, and joy; but to the sinner he giveth travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him that pleaseth God. This also is vanity and a striving after ind.
For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:
a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that hich is planted;
a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break don, and a time to build up;
a time to eep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
a time to cast aay stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;
a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast aay;
a time to rend, and a time to se; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;
a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for ar, and a time for peace.
What profit hath he that orketh in that herein he laboreth?
I have seen the travail hich God hath given to the sons of men to be exercised thereith.
He hath made everything beautiful in its time: also he hath set eternity in their heart, yet so that man cannot find out the ork that God hath done from the beginning even to the end.
I kno that there is nothing better for them, than to rejoice, and to do good so long as they live.
And also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy good in all his labor, is the gift of God.
I kno that, hatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor anything taken from it; and God hath done it, that men should fear before him.
That hich is hath been long ago; and that hich is to be hath long ago been: and God seeketh again that hich is passed aay.
And moreover I sa under the sun, in the place of justice, that ickedness as there; and in the place of righteousness, that ickedness as there.
I said in my heart, God ill judge the righteous and the icked; for there is a time there for every purpose and for every ork.
I said in my heart, \add It is\add* because of the sons of men, that God may prove them, and that they may see that they themselves are \add but as\add* beasts.

For that hich befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; and man hath no preeminence above the beasts: for all is vanity.
All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again.
Who knoeth the spirit of man, hether it goeth upard, and the spirit of the beast, hether it goeth donard to the earth?
Wherefore I sa that there is nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his orks; for that is his portion: for ho shall bring him \add back\add* to see hat shall be after him?

Then I returned and sa all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and, behold, the tears of such as ere oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there as poer; but they had no comforter.
Wherefore I praised the dead that have been long dead more than the living that are yet alive;
yea, better than them both \add did I esteem\add* him that hath not yet been, ho hath not seen the evil ork that is done under the sun.
Then I sa all labor and every skilful ork, that for this a man is envied of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after ind.
The fool foldeth his hands together, and eateth his on flesh.
Better is a handful, ith quietness, than to handfuls ith labor and striving after ind.
Then I returned and sa vanity under the sun.

There is one that is alone, and he hath not a second; yea, he hath neither son nor brother; yet is there no end of all his labor, neither are his eyes satisfied ith riches. For hom then, \add saith he\add*, do I labor, and deprive my soul of good? This also is vanity, yea, it is a sore travail.
To are better than one, because they have a good reard for their labor.
For if they fall, the one ill lift up his fello; but oe to him that is alone hen he falleth, and hath not another to lift him up.
Again, if to lie together, then they have armth; but ho can one be arm \add alone\add*?
And if a man prevail against him that is alone, to shall ithstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
Better is a poor and ise youth than an old and foolish king, ho knoeth not ho to receive admonition any more.
For out of prison he came forth to be king; yea, even in his kingdom he as born poor.
I sa all the living that alk under the sun, that they ere ith the youth, the second, that stood up in his stead.
There as no end of all the people, even of all them over hom he as: yet they that come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after ind.
Keep thy foot hen thou goest to the house of God; for to dra nigh to hear is better than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they kno not that they do evil.
Be not rash ith thy mouth, and let not thy heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy ords be fe.
For a dream cometh ith a multitude of business, and a fool’s voice ith a multitude of ords.
When thou voest a vo unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that hich thou voest.
Better is it that thou shouldest not vo, than that thou shouldest vo and not pay.
Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it as an error: herefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the ork of thy hands?
For in the multitude of dreams there are vanities, and in many ords: but fear thou God.

If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and the violent taking aay of justice and righteousness in a province, marvel not at the matter: for one higher than the high regardeth; and there are higher than they.
Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king \add himself\add* is served by the field.
He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied ith silver; nor he that loveth abundance, ith increase: this also is vanity.
When goods increase, they are increased that eat them; and hat advantage is there to the oner thereof, save the beholding \add of them\add* ith his eyes?
The sleep of a laboring man is seet, hether he eat little or much; but the fulness of the rich ill not suffer him to sleep.
There is a grievous evil hich I have seen under the sun, \add namely\add*, riches kept by the oner thereof to his hurt:
and those riches perish by evil adventure; and if he hath begotten a son, there is nothing in his hand.
As he came forth from his mother’s omb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor, hich he may carry aay in his hand.
And this also is a grievous evil, that in all points as he came, so shall he go: and hat profit hath he that he laboreth for the ind?
All his days also he eateth in darkness, and he is sore vexed, and hath sickness and rath.

Behold, that hich I have seen to be good and to be comely is for one to eat and to drink, and to enjoy good in all his labor, herein he laboreth under the sun, all the days of his life hich God hath given him: for this is his portion.
Every man also to hom God hath given riches and ealth, and hath given him poer to eat thereof, and to take his portion, and to rejoice in his labor— this is the gift of God.
For he shall not much remember the days of his life; because God ansereth \add him\add* in the joy of his heart.
There is an evil hich I have seen under the sun, and it is heavy upon men:

a man to hom God giveth riches, ealth, and honor, so that he lacketh nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not poer to eat thereof, but an alien eateth it; this is vanity, and it is an evil disease.

If a man beget a hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul be not filled ith good, and moreover he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he:
for it cometh in vanity, and departeth in darkness, and the name thereof is covered ith darkness;
moreover it hath not seen the sun nor knon it; this hath rest rather than the other:
yea, though he live a thousand years tice told, and yet enjoy no good, do not all go to one place?
All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled.
For hat advantage hath the ise more than the fool? \add or\add* hat hath the poor man, that knoeth ho to alk before the living?
Better is the sight of the eyes than the andering of the desire: this also is vanity and a striving after ind.
Whatsoever hath been, the name thereof as given long ago; and it is knon hat man is; neither can he contend ith him that is mightier than he.
Seeing there are many things that increase vanity, hat is man the better?
For ho knoeth hat is good for man in \add his\add* life, all the days of his vain life hich he spendeth as a shado? for ho can tell a man hat shall be after him under the sun?
A \add good\add* name is better than precious oil; and the day of death, than the day of one’s birth.
It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living ill lay it to his heart.
Sorro is better than laughter; for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made glad.
The heart of the ise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.
It is better to hear the rebuke of the ise, than for a man to hear the song of fools.
For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool: this also is vanity.
Surely extortion maketh the ise man foolish; and a bribe destroyeth the understanding.
Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof; \add and\add* the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.
Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry; for anger resteth in the bosom of fools.
Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days ere better than these? for thou dost not inquire isely concerning this.
Wisdom is as good as an inheritance; yea, more excellent is it for them that see the sun.
For isdom is a defence, even as money is a defence; but the excellency of knoledge is, that isdom preserveth the life of him that hath it.
Consider the ork of God: for ho can make that straight, hich he hath made crooked?

In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider; yea, God hath made the one side by side ith the other, to the end that man should not find out anything \add that shall be\add* after him.
All this have I seen in my days of vanity: there is a righteous man that perisheth in his righteousness, and there is a icked man that prolongeth \add his life\add* in his evil-doing.
Be not righteous overmuch; neither make thyself overise: hy shouldest thou destroy thyself?
Be not overmuch icked, neither be thou foolish: hy shouldest thou die before thy time?
It is good that thou shouldest take hold of this; yea, also from that ithdra not thy hand: for he that feareth God shall come forth from them all.
Wisdom is a strength to the ise man more than ten rulers that are in a city.
Surely there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not.
Also take not heed unto all ords that are spoken, lest thou hear thy servant curse thee;
for oftentimes also thine on heart knoeth that thou thyself likeise hast cursed others.
All this have I proved in isdom: I said, I ill be ise; but it as far from me.
That hich is, is far off and exceeding deep; ho can find it out?
I turned about, and my heart \add as set\add* to kno and to search out, and to seek isdom and the reason \add of things\add*, and to kno that ickedness is folly, and that foolishness is madness.
And I find more bitter than death the oman hose heart is snares and nets, \add and\add* hose hands are bands: hoso pleaseth God shall escape from her; but the sinner shall be taken by her.
Behold, this have I found, saith the Preacher, \add laying\add* one thing to another, to find out the account;
hich my soul still seeketh, but I have not found: one man among a thousand have I found; but a oman among all those have I not found.
Behold, this only have I found: that God made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.
Who is as the ise man? and ho knoeth the interpretation of a thing? A man’s isdom maketh his face to shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.
I \add counsel thee\add*, Keep the king’s command, and that in regard of the oath of God.
Be not hasty to go out of his presence; persist not in an evil thing: for he doeth hatsoever pleaseth him.
For the king’s ord \add hath\add* poer; and ho may say unto him, What doest thou?
Whoso keepeth the commandment shall kno no evil thing; and a ise man’s heart discerneth time and judgment:
for to every purpose there is a time and judgment; because the misery of man is great upon him:
for he knoeth not that hich shall be; for ho can tell him ho it shall be?

There is no man that hath poer over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he poer over the day of death; and there is no discharge in ar: neither shall ickedness deliver him that is given to it.
All this have I seen, and applied my heart unto every ork that is done under the sun: \add there is\add* a time herein one man hath poer over another to his hurt.
So I sa the icked buried, and they came \add to the grave\add*; and they that had done right ent aay from the holy place, and ere forgotten in the city: this also is vanity.
Because sentence against an evil ork is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.
Though a sinner do evil a hundred times, and prolong his \add days\add*, yet surely I kno that it shall be ell ith them that fear God, that fear before him:
but it shall not be ell ith the icked, neither shall he prolong \add his\add* days, \add hich are\add* as a shado; because he feareth not before God.

There is a vanity hich is done upon the earth, that there are righteous men unto hom it happeneth according to the ork of the icked; again, there are icked men to hom it happeneth according to the ork of the righteous: I said that this also is vanity.

Then I commended mirth, because a man hath no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be joyful: for that shall abide ith him in his labor \add all\add* the days of his life hich God hath given him under the sun.
When I applied my heart to kno isdom, and to see the business that is done upon the earth ( for also there is that neither day nor night seeth sleep ith his eyes),

then I beheld all the ork of God, that man cannot find out the ork that is done under the sun: because hoever much a man labor to seek it out, yet he shall not find it; yea moreover, though a ise man think to kno it, yet shall he not be able to find it.
For all this I laid to my heart, even to explore all this: that the righteous, and the ise, and their orks, are in the hand of God; hether it be love or hatred, man knoeth it not; all is before them.

All things come alike to all: there is one event to the righteous and to the icked; to the good and to the clean and to the unclean; to him that sacrificeth and to him that sacrificeth not; as is the good, so is the sinner; \add and\add* he that seareth, as he that feareth an oath.

This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that there is one event unto all: yea also, the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart hile they live, and after that \add they go\add* to the dead.
For to him that is joined ith all the living there is hope; for a living dog is better than a dead lion.
For the living kno that they shall die: but the dead kno not anything, neither have they any more a reard; for the memory of them is forgotten.
As ell their love, as their hatred and their envy, is perished long ago; neither have they any more a portion for ever in anything that is done under the sun.
Go thy ay, eat thy bread ith joy, and drink thy ine ith a merry heart; for God hath already accepted thy orks.
Let thy garments be alays hite; and let not thy head lack oil.

Live joyfully ith the ife hom thou lovest all the days of thy life of vanity, hich he hath given thee under the sun, all thy days of vanity: for that is thy portion in life, and in thy labor herein thou laborest under the sun.
Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do \add it\add* ith thy might; for there is no ork, nor device, nor knoledge, nor isdom, in Sheol, hither thou goest.

I returned, and sa under the sun, that the race is not to the sift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the ise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favor to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.

For man also knoeth not his time: as the fishes that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare, even so are the sons of men snared in an evil time, hen it falleth suddenly upon them.
I have also seen isdom under the sun on this ise, and it seemed great unto me:
There as a little city, and fe men ithin it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bularks against it.
No there as found in it a poor ise man, and he by his isdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man.
Then said I, Wisdom is better than strength: nevertheless the poor man’s isdom is despised, and his ords are not heard.
The ords of the ise heard in quiet are better than the cry of him that ruleth among fools.
Wisdom is better than eapons of ar; but one sinner destroyeth much good.
Dead flies cause the oil of the perfumer to send forth an evil odor; \add so\add* doth a little folly outeigh isdom and honor.
A ise man’s heart is at his right hand; but a fool’s heart at his left.
Yea also, hen the fool alketh by the ay, his understanding faileth him, and he saith to every one \add that\add* he is a fool.
If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place; for gentleness allayeth great offences.
There is an evil hich I have seen under the sun, as it ere an error hich proceedeth from the ruler:
folly is set in great dignity, and the rich sit in a lo place.
I have seen servants upon horses, and princes alking like servants upon the earth.
He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and hoso breaketh through a all, a serpent shall bite him.
Whoso heeth out stones shall be hurt thereith; \add and\add* he that cleaveth ood is endangered thereby.
If the iron be blunt, and one do not het the edge, then must he put to more strength: but isdom is profitable to direct.
If the serpent bite before it is charmed, then is there no advantage in the charmer.
The ords of a ise man’s mouth are gracious; but the lips of a fool ill sallo up himself.
The beginning of the ords of his mouth is foolishness; and the end of his talk is mischievous madness.
A fool also multiplieth ords: \add yet\add* man knoeth not hat shall be; and that hich shall be after him, ho can tell him?
The labor of fools earieth every one of them; for he knoeth not ho to go to the city.
Woe to thee, O land, hen thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning!
Happy art thou, O land, hen thy king is the son of nobles, and thy princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness!
By slothfulness the roof sinketh in; and through idleness of the hands the house leaketh.
A feast is made for laughter, and ine maketh glad the life; and money ansereth all things.
Revile not the king, no, not in thy thought; and revile not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the heavens shall carry the voice, and that hich hath ings shall tell the matter.
Cast thy bread upon the aters; for thou shalt find it after many days.
Give a portion to seven, yea, even unto eight; for thou knoest not hat evil shall be upon the earth.
If the clouds be full of rain, they empty themselves upon the earth; and if a tree fall toard the south, or toard the north, in the place here the tree falleth, there shall it be.
He that observeth the ind shall not so; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.
As thou knoest not hat is the ay of the ind, \add nor\add* ho the bones \add do gro\add* in the omb of her that is ith child; even so thou knoest not the ork of God ho doeth all.
In the morning so thy seed, and in the evening ithhold not thy hand; for thou knoest not hich shall prosper, hether this or that, or hether they both shall be alike good.
Truly the light is seet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun.
Yea, if a man live many years, let him rejoice in them all; but let him remember the days of darkness, for they shall be many. All that cometh is vanity.

Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth, and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and alk in the ays of thy heart, and in the sight of thine eyes; but kno thou, that for all these things God ill bring thee into judgment.
Therefore remove sorro from thy heart, and put aay evil from thy flesh; for youth and the dan of life are vanity.
Remember also thy Creator in the days of thy youth, before the evil days come, and the years dra nigh, hen thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
before the sun, and the light, and the moon, and the stars, are darkened, and the clouds return after the rain;
in the day hen the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bo themselves, and the grinders cease because they are fe, and those that look out of the indos shall be darkened,
and the doors shall be shut in the street; hen the sound of the grinding is lo, and one shall rise up at the voice of a bird, and all the daughters of music shall be brought lo;

yea, they shall be afraid of \add that hich is\add* high, and terrors \add shall be\add* in the ay; and the almond-tree shall blossom, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail; because man goeth to his everlasting home, and the mourners go about the streets:
before the silver cord is loosed, or the golden bol is broken, or the pitcher is broken at the fountain, or the heel broken at the cistern,
and the dust returneth to the earth as it as, and the spirit returneth unto God ho gave it.
Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; all is vanity.
And further, because the Preacher as ise, he still taught the people knoledge; yea, he pondered, and sought out, \add and\add* set in order many proverbs.
The Preacher sought to find out acceptable ords, and that hich as ritten uprightly, \add even\add* ords of truth.
The ords of the ise are as goads; and as nails ell fastened are \add the ords of\add* the masters of assemblies, \add hich\add* are given from one shepherd.
And furthermore, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a eariness of the flesh.
\add This is\add* the end of the matter; all hath been heard: Fear God, and keep his commandments; for this is the hole \add duty\add* of man.
For God ill bring every ork into judgment, ith every hidden thing, hether it be good, or hether it be evil.
The Song of songs, hich is Solomon’s. \b
Let him kiss me ith the kisses of his mouth; For thy love is better than ine.
Thine oils have a goodly fragrance; Thy name is \add as\add* oil poured forth; Therefore do the virgins love thee.
Dra me; e ill run after thee: The king hath brought me into his chambers; We ill be glad and rejoice in thee; We ill make mention of thy love more than of ine: Rightly do they love thee. \b
I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, As the tents of Kedar, As the curtains of Solomon.

Look not upon me, because I am sarthy, Because the sun hath scorched me. My mother’s sons ere incensed against me; They made me keeper of the vineyards; \add But\add* mine on vineyard have I not kept.

Tell me, O thou hom my soul loveth, Where thou feedest \add thy flock\add*, Where thou makest \add it\add* to rest at noon: For hy should I be as one that is veiled Beside the flocks of thy companions? \b
If thou kno not, O thou fairest among omen, Go thy ay forth by the footsteps of the flock, And feed thy kids beside the shepherds’ tents. \b
I have compared thee, O my love, To a steed in Pharaoh’s chariots.
Thy cheeks are comely ith plaits \add of hair\add*, Thy neck ith strings of jeels.
We ill make thee plaits of gold With studs of silver. \b
While the king sat at his table, My spikenard sent forth its fragrance.
My beloved is unto me \add as\add* a bundle of myrrh, That lieth betixt my breasts.
My beloved is unto me \add as\add* a cluster of henna-floers In the vineyards of En-gedi. \b
Behold, thou art fair, my love; Behold thou art fair; Thine eyes are \add as\add* doves. \b
Behold, thou art fair, my beloved, yea, pleasant: Also our couch is green.
The beams of our house are cedars, \add And\add* our rafters are firs.
I am a rose of Sharon, A lily of the valleys. \b
As a lily among thorns, So is my love among the daughters. \b
As the apple-tree among the trees of the ood, So is my beloved among the sons. I sat don under his shado ith great delight, And his fruit as seet to my taste.
He brought me to the banqueting-house, And his banner over me as love.
Stay ye me ith raisins, refresh me ith apples; For I am sick from love.
His left hand \add is\add* under my head, And his right hand doth embrace me. \b
I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, By the roes, or by the hinds of the field, That ye stir not up, nor aake \add my\add* love, Until he please. \b
The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh, Leaping upon the mountains, Skipping upon the hills.
My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: Behold, he standeth behind our all; He looketh in at the indos; He glanceth through the lattice. \b
My beloved spake, and said unto me, Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come aay.
For, lo, the inter is past; The rain is over and gone;
The floers appear on the earth; The time of the singing \add of birds\add* is come, And the voice of the turtle-dove is heard in our land;
The fig-tree ripeneth her green figs, And the vines are in blossom; They give forth their fragrance. Arise, my love, my fair one, and come aay.
O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, In the covert of the steep place, Let me see thy countenance, Let me hear thy voice; For seet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely. \b
Take us the foxes, the little foxes, That spoil the vineyards; For our vineyards are in blossom.
My beloved is mine, and I am his: He feedeth \add his flock\add* among the lilies.
Until the day be cool, and the shados flee aay, Turn, my beloved, and be thou like a roe or a young hart Upon the mountains of Bether. \b
By night on my bed I sought him hom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.
\add I said\add*, I ill rise no, and go about the city; In the streets and in the broad ays I ill seek him hom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.
The atchmen that go about the city found me; \add To hom I said\add*, Sa ye him hom my soul loveth?

It as but a little that I passed from them, When I found him hom my soul loveth: I held him, and ould not let him go, Until I had brought him into my mother’s house, And into the chamber of her that conceived me. \b
I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, By the roes, or by the hinds of the field, That ye stir not up, nor aake \add my\add* love, Until he please. \b
Who is this that cometh up from the ilderness Like pillars of smoke, Perfumed ith myrrh and frankincense, With all poders of the merchant? \b
Behold, it is the litter of Solomon; Threescore mighty men are about it, Of the mighty men of Israel.
They all handle the sord, \add and\add* are expert in ar: Every man hath his sord upon his thigh, Because of fear in the night.
King Solomon made himself a palanquin Of the ood of Lebanon.
He made the pillars thereof of silver, The bottom thereof of gold, the seat of it of purple, The midst thereof being paved ith love, From the daughters of Jerusalem.
Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon, With the cron hereith his mother hath croned him In the day of his espousals, And in the day of the gladness of his heart. \b
Behold, thou art fair, my love; behold, thou art fair; Thine eyes are \add as\add* doves behind thy veil. Thy hair is as a flock of goats, That lie along the side of mount Gilead.
Thy teeth are like a flock \add of ees\add* that are \add nely\add* shorn, Which are come up from the ashing, Whereof every one hath tins, And none is bereaved among them.
Thy lips are like a thread of scarlet, And thy mouth is comely. Thy temples are like a piece of a pomegranate Behind thy veil.
Thy neck is like the toer of David Builded for an armory, Whereon there hang a thousand bucklers, All the shields of the mighty men.
Thy to breasts are like to fans That are tins of a roe, Which feed among the lilies. \b
Until the day be cool, and the shados flee aay, I ill get me to the mountain of myrrh, And to the hill of frankincense. \b
Thou art all fair, my love; And there is no spot in thee.
Come ith me from Lebanon, \add my\add* bride, With me from Lebanon: Look from the top of Amana, From the top of Senir and Hermon, From the lions’ dens, From the mountains of the leopards.
Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, \add my\add* bride; Thou hast ravished my heart ith one of thine eyes, With one chain of thy neck.
Ho fair is thy love, my sister, \add my\add* bride! Ho much better is thy love than ine! And the fragrance of thine oils than all manner of spices!
Thy lips, O \add my\add* bride, drop \add as\add* the honeycomb: Honey and milk are under thy tongue; And the smell of thy garments is like the smell of Lebanon.
A garden shut up is my sister, \add my\add* bride; A spring shut up, a fountain sealed.
Thy shoots are an orchard of pomegranates, ith precious fruits; Henna ith spikenard plants,
Spikenard and saffron, Calamus and cinnamon, ith all trees of frankincense; Myrrh and aloes, ith all the chief spices.
\add Thou art\add* a fountain of gardens, A ell of living aters, And floing streams from Lebanon. \b
Aake, O north ind; and come, thou south; Blo upon my garden, that the spices thereof may flo out. Let my beloved come into his garden, And eat his precious fruits. \b

I am come into my garden, my sister, \add my\add* bride: I have gathered my myrrh ith my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb ith my honey; I have drunk my ine ith my milk. Eat, O friends; Drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved. \b

I as asleep, but my heart aked: It is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, \add saying\add*, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled; For my head is filled ith de, My locks ith the drops of the night.
I have put off my garment; ho shall I put it on? I have ashed my feet; ho shall I defile them?
My beloved put in his hand by the hole \add of the door\add*, And my heart as moved for him.
I rose up to open to my beloved; And my hands dropped ith myrrh, And my fingers ith liquid myrrh, Upon the handles of the bolt.
I opened to my beloved; But my beloved had ithdran himself, \add and\add* as gone. My soul had failed me hen he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no anser.
The atchmen that go about the city found me, They smote me, they ounded me; The keepers of the alls took aay my mantle from me.
I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, If ye find my beloved, That ye tell him, that I am sick from love. \b
What is thy beloved more than \add another\add* beloved, O thou fairest among omen? What is thy beloved more than \add another\add* beloved, That thou dost so adjure us? \b
My beloved is hite and ruddy, The chiefest among ten thousand.
His head is \add as\add* the most fine gold; His locks are bushy, \add and\add* black as a raven.
His eyes are like doves beside the ater-brooks, Washed ith milk, \add and\add* fitly set.
His cheeks are as a bed of spices, \add As\add* banks of seet herbs: His lips are \add as\add* lilies, dropping liquid myrrh.
His hands are \add as\add* rings of gold set ith beryl: His body is \add as\add* ivory ork overlaid \add ith\add* sapphires.
His legs are \add as\add* pillars of marble, set upon sockets of fine gold: His aspect is like Lebanon, excellent as the cedars.
His mouth is most seet; Yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem. \b
Whither is thy beloved gone, O thou fairest among omen? Whither hath thy beloved turned him, That e may seek him ith thee? \b
My beloved is gone don to his garden, To the beds of spices, To feed in the gardens, and to gather lilies.
I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine: He feedeth \add his flock\add* among the lilies. \b
Thou art fair, O my love, as Tirzah, Comely as Jerusalem, Terrible as an army ith banners.
Turn aay thine eyes from me, For they have overcome me. Thy hair is as a flock of goats, That lie along the side of Gilead.
Thy teeth are like a flock of ees, Which are come up from the ashing; Whereof every one hath tins, And none is bereaved among them.
Thy temples are like a piece of a pomegranate Behind thy veil.
There are threescore queens, and fourscore concubines, And virgins ithout number.

My dove, my undefiled, is \add but\add* one; She is the only one of her mother; She is the choice one of her that bare her. The daughters sa her, and called her blessed; \add Yea\add*, the queens and the concubines, and they praised her. \b
Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, Fair as the moon, Clear as the sun, Terrible as an army ith banners? \b
I ent don into the garden of nuts, To see the green plants of the valley, To see hether the vine budded, \add And\add* the pomegranates ere in floer.
Before I as aare, my soul set me \add Among\add* the chariots of my princely people. \b
Return, return, O Shulammite; Return, return, that e may look upon thee. \b Why ill ye look upon the Shulammite, As upon the dance of Mahanaim? \b
Ho beautiful are thy feet in sandals, O prince’s daughter! Thy rounded thighs are like jeels, The ork of the hands of a skilful orkman.
Thy body is \add like\add* a round goblet, \add Wherein\add* no mingled ine is anting: Thy aist is \add like\add* a heap of heat Set about ith lilies.
Thy to breasts are like to fans That are tins of a roe.
Thy neck is like the toer of ivory; Thine eyes \add as\add* the pools in Heshbon, By the gate of Bath-rabbim; Thy nose is like the toer of Lebanon Which looketh toard Damascus.
Thy head upon thee is like Carmel, And the hair of thy head like purple; The king is held captive in the tresses \add thereof\add*.
Ho fair and ho pleasant art thou, O love, for delights!
This thy stature is like to a palm-tree, And thy breasts to its clusters.
I said, I ill climb up into the palm-tree, I ill take hold of the branches thereof: Let thy breasts be as clusters of the vine, And the smell of thy breath like apples,
And thy mouth like the best ine, That goeth don smoothly for my beloved, Gliding through the lips of those that are asleep. \b
I am my beloved’s; And his desire is toard me.
Come, my beloved, let us go forth into the field; Let us lodge in the villages.
Let us get up early to the vineyards; Let us see hether the vine hath budded, \add And\add* its blossom is open, \add And\add* the pomegranates are in floer: There ill I give thee my love.
The mandrakes give forth fragrance; And at our doors are all manner of precious fruits, ne and old, Which I have laid up for thee, O my beloved.
Oh that thou ert as my brother, That sucked the breasts of my mother! \add When\add* I should find thee ithout, I ould kiss thee; Yea, and none ould despise me.
I ould lead thee, \add and\add* bring thee into my mother’s house, Who ould instruct me; I ould cause thee to drink of spiced ine, Of the juice of my pomegranate.
His left hand \add should be\add* under my head, And his right hand should embrace me. \b
I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, That ye stir not up, nor aake \add my\add* love, Until he please. \b

Who is this that cometh up from the ilderness, Leaning upon her beloved? \b Under the apple-tree I aakened thee: There thy mother as in travail ith thee, There as she in travail that brought thee forth. \b
Set me as a seal upon thy heart, As a seal upon thine arm: For love is strong as death; Jealousy is cruel as Sheol; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of Jehovah.
Many aters cannot quench love, Neither can floods dron it: If a man ould give all the substance of his house for love, He ould utterly be contemned. \b
We have a little sister, And she hath no breasts: What shall e do for our sister In the day hen she shall be spoken for? \b
If she be a all, We ill build upon her a turret of silver: And if she be a door, We ill inclose her ith boards of cedar. \b
I am a all, and my breasts like the toers \add thereof\add*: Then as I in his eyes as one that found peace.
Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon; He let out the vineyard unto keepers; Every one for the fruit thereof as to bring a thousand \add pieces\add* of silver.
My vineyard, hich is mine, is before me: Thou, O Solomon, shalt have the thousand, And those that keep the fruit thereof to hundred. \b
Thou that dellest in the gardens, The companions hearken for thy voice: Cause me to hear it. \b
Make haste, my beloved, And be thou like to a roe or to a young hart Upon the mountains of spices.
The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, hich he sa concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.
Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth; for Jehovah hath spoken: I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me.
The ox knoeth his oner, and the ass his master’s crib; \add but\add* Israel doth not kno, my people doth not consider.

Ah sinful nation, a people laden ith iniquity, a seed of evil-doers, children that deal corruptly! they have forsaken Jehovah, they have despised the Holy One of Israel, they are estranged \add and gone\add* backard.
Why ill ye be still stricken, that ye revolt more and more? the hole head is sick, and the hole heart faint.
From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; \add but\add* ounds, and bruises, and fresh stripes: they have not been closed, neither bound up, neither mollified ith oil.
Your country is desolate; your cities are burned ith fire; your land, strangers devour it in your presence, and it is desolate, as overthron by strangers.
And the daughter of Zion is left as a booth in a vineyard, as a lodge in a garden of cucumbers, as a besieged city.
Except Jehovah of hosts had left unto us a very small remnant, e should have been as Sodom, e should have been like unto Gomorrah.
Hear the ord of Jehovah, ye rulers of Sodom; give ear unto the la of our God, ye people of Gomorrah.

What unto me is the multitude of your sacrifices? saith Jehovah: I have had enough of the burnt-offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he-goats.
When ye come to appear before me, ho hath required this at your hand, to trample my courts?
Bring no more vain oblations; incense is an abomination unto me; ne moon and sabbath, the calling of assemblies,— I cannot aay ith iniquity and the solemn meeting.
Your ne moons and your appointed feasts my soul hateth; they are a trouble unto me; I am eary of bearing them.
And hen ye spread forth your hands, I ill hide mine eyes from you; yea, hen ye make many prayers, I ill not hear: your hands are full of blood.
Wash you, make you clean; put aay the evil of your doings from before mine eyes; cease to do evil;
learn to do ell; seek justice, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the ido.
Come no, and let us reason together, saith Jehovah: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as hite as sno; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as ool.
If ye be illing and obedient, ye shall eat the good of the land:
but if ye refuse and rebel, ye shall be devoured ith the sord; for the mouth of Jehovah hath spoken it.
Ho is the faithful city become a harlot! she that as full of justice! righteousness lodged in her, but no murderers.
Thy silver is become dross, thy ine mixed ith ater.
Thy princes are rebellious, and companions of thieves; every one loveth bribes, and folloeth after reards: they judge not the fatherless, neither doth the cause of the ido come unto them.
Therefore saith the Lord, Jehovah of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel, Ah, I ill ease me of mine adversaries, and avenge me of mine enemies;
and I ill turn my hand upon thee, and thoroughly purge aay thy dross, and ill take aay all thy tin;
and I ill restore thy judges as at the first, and thy counsellors as at the beginning: afterard thou shalt be called The city of righteousness, a faithful ton.
Zion shall be redeemed ith justice, and her converts ith righteousness.
But the destruction of transgressors and sinners shall be together, and they that forsake Jehovah shall be consumed.
For they shall be ashamed of the oaks hich ye have desired, and ye shall be confounded for the gardens that ye have chosen.
For ye shall be as an oak hose leaf fadeth, and as a garden that hath no ater.
And the strong shall be as to, and his ork as a spark; and they shall both burn together, and none shall quench them. \b
